passages.t: Write down the date: the pot on the fire
passages.happening:
In the ninth year, on the tenth day of the tenth month, God says, ‘Son of man, write down today’s date, for on this very day the king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem’ (verse 2). Then he gives a parable: ‘Put the pot on the fire; put it on and pour in the water’ (verse 3). Choice pieces of meat go in, and it boils (verses 4-5).

‘Woe to the city of bloodshed, to the pot now rusted’ (verse 6). Its blood lies on bare rock, uncovered (verses 7-8). God will heap on the wood and boil the pot dry, then set it empty on the coals until its corrosion burns away (verses 9-11). ‘I tried to cleanse you, but you would not be purified from your filthiness’ (verse 13). He will not relent (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The date is the same day 2 Kings and Jeremiah give for the start of Nebuchadnezzar's siege: on the usual reckoning, January 588 BC, though some scholars place it a year later. Ezekiel was hundreds of miles away in Babylonia. He is told to write the date down, so that when news came, the record would show he had known on the day itself. After the exile there was a fast in the tenth month, and Jewish tradition still keeps a fast in memory of the siege.

The pot takes up the leaders' own saying in 11:3, that the city is the pot and they are the meat. God turns it against them. The law required that the blood of a slaughtered animal be poured out and covered with dust. Blood left on bare rock was blood unacknowledged, crying out like Abel's.
passages.later: ‘On the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem’ (2 Kings 25:1). Abel's blood cried out to God from the ground (Genesis 4:10).
passages.asks: God tried to cleanse the city, and it would not be cleansed. Ask where you have resisted God's work of making you clean. And ask what you would need to let go of for him to do it.

passages.t: The death of the desire of his eyes
passages.happening:
‘Son of man, behold, I am about to take away the desire of your eyes with a fatal blow. But you must not mourn or weep or let your tears flow’ (verse 16). He is to groan quietly and not keep the customs of mourning (verse 17). ‘So I spoke to the people in the morning, and in the evening my wife died. And the next morning I did as I had been commanded’ (verse 18).

The people ask what this means (verse 19). God answers that he is about to profane his sanctuary, ‘the pride of your power, the desire of your eyes, and the delight of your soul’ (verse 21), and their sons and daughters will fall by the sword. They will do as Ezekiel has done: they will not mourn openly, but will waste away and groan among themselves (verses 22-23). ‘Thus Ezekiel will be a sign for you’ (verse 24). On the day a fugitive brings the news, Ezekiel's mouth will be opened (verses 25-27).
passages.hearers:
The customs Ezekiel was told not to keep were well known. Mourners removed their headdress and sandals, covered their lips, wailed in public, and ate food brought by neighbors, the bread of mourners.

The temple was the desire of Israel's eyes, as Ezekiel's wife was the desire of his. When the news came, the loss would be too great for any ritual. The people's stunned silence would match the prophet's.

This is the only time Ezekiel's wife appears in the book, and she is not named. The silence imposed in chapter 3 ends when the news of the city's fall arrives (33:21-22).
passages.later: Job said in his grief, ‘The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away’ (Job 1:21). The fast of the tenth month would one day become a feast (Zechariah 8:19).
passages.hard:
Did God really take Ezekiel's wife to make a point, and why forbid him to grieve?

The text is stark, and readers rightly flinch. Some interpreters read God's words as foreknowledge rather than cause: God tells his prophet that his wife will die and directs how that death, already approaching, will become a sign. Others accept that the text presents the death as God's act and place it within the Bible's wider confession that life and death are in God's hands, without claiming to explain why this woman died when she did.

It matters what is forbidden. Ezekiel is told to groan quietly (verse 17). He is not told to feel nothing. He is told not to perform the public rituals of mourning, so that his silence would become a sign of the stunned grief of people whose loss is too great for ritual. Many readers find this one of the most human passages in the book, because it shows what the prophet paid.

It is not a teaching that believers must hold back grief. Scripture gives grief full voice, in the psalms of lament, in Lamentations, and in Jesus weeping at the grave of Lazarus (John 11:35).
passages.asks: Ezekiel lost the desire of his eyes and still did what God asked. Ask what you love most in this world. And ask how you would hold on to God if you lost it.
